GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
DEPARTMENT OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
 
LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 1579 
  ANSWERED ON 28/07/2026 
 
CONNECTIVITY WITH ALL-WEATHER ROADS UNDER PMGSY 
 
1579. Shri Malaiyarasan D: 
 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 
(a)  the details of roads constructed, upgraded, total length of roads 
completed and the expenditure incurred under the Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) during the last five years, 
State/UT-wise including Kallakurichi Lok Sabha Constituency of 
Tamil Nadu; 
(b)  the number of eligible habitations that have been provided all-
weather road connectivity under PMGSY and the number of 
habitations still pending for connectivity, State and UT-wise; 
(c)  whether the Government has conducted any assessment of the 
quality, durability and maintenance status of roads constructed 
under PMGSY, if so, the details thereof, including the number of 
roads requiring repair or reconstruction; 
(d)  the details of funds allocated, released and utilised under 
PMGSY during the last five years; and 
(e)  the steps taken by the Government to ensure timely completion 
of pending road projects, improve monitoring through digital 
platforms, maintain road quality and address grievances of rural 
communities regarding PMGSY roads? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI KAMLESH PASWAN)  
  
(a):  In the country including the State of Tamil Nadu, a total of 
1,31,589 km road length (18,814 roads and 5,110 bridges) was 
completed at an expenditure of Rs. 1,07,942 crore (including State 
Share), during the last five years, under various verticals of Pradhan 

Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY). The year wise details are given 
below:-  
  
Financial 
Year 
No. of Roads Length  
(in km) 
No. of Bridges Expenditure  
(in Rs. Crores) 
2021-22 6557 42015 1398 27833 
2022-23 6074 29721 1101 24228 
2023-24 443 26095 857 20301 
2024-25 2835 18110 712 18672 
2025-26 2905 15648 1042 14914 
Total 18814 131589 5110 105948 
  
Since inception, in Kallakurichi Constituency of Tamil Nadu, 62 roads 
of 257 km length and 3 bridges have been constructed with an 
expenditure of Rs.184 crore under various verticals of the PMGSY. 
The State/UT-wise, District-wise and Parliamentary Constituency-
wise details of rural road projects and the stages of construction 
under various verticals of PMGSY may be accessed at the programme 
website https://pmgsy.dord.gov.in/dbweb on a real-time basis.  
  
(b):  Under PMGSY-I, out of total 1,63,275 sanctioned habitations, 
162,845 habitations (99.7%) have been provided connectivity. The 
road works for providing connectivity to balance 401 habitations are 
at various stages of execution. 
 
In September 2024, the Government of India launched PMGSY 
IV. The primary objective of PMGSY IV is to provide all-weather road 
connectivity to about 25,000 unconnected habitations of population 
size (as per Census 2011) 500+ in plains, 250+ in Special Category 
States (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Ladakh, Manipur, Meghalaya, 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu 
Kashmir and Uttarakhand), Special Category Areas [(Tribal Schedule-
V Areas, Desert Areas, Aspirational Blocks/ Districts and Hilly areas 
as notified by the respective State Government (cross slope more 
than 25% gradient and the elevation is more than 600 meters from 
the Mean Sea Level)] and 100+ in LWE affected Districts including 
Legacy & Thrust Districts identified by MHA from time to time. Under 
PMGSY-IV, habitations identified under VVP-II are being prioritised for 
all-weather road connectivity. Under PMGSY IV, the States/UTs have 
surveyed 41,200 habitations for connectivity which are further 

scrutinized by National Rural Infrastructure Development Agency 
(NRIDA) and sanctions are given based on the Detailed Project 
Reports sent by the State/UTs. Till date, 6752 road works of 19,643 
km and 94 bridges have been sanctioned which will provide 
connectivity to 7455 habitations.  
 
(c):  As per PMGSY guidelines, ensuring the quality of road works and 
maintenance of roads constructed is the responsibility of the 
State/UT Governments. However, the Department of Rural 
Development conducts quality assessment through National Quality 
Monitors (NQMs) and monitors maintenance of roads and bridges 
through compulsory routine inspections on the eMARG digital 
platform.  
 
All PMGSY works are covered by initial five year maintenance 
contracts during the Defect Liability Period (DLP) as per the Standard 
Bidding Document. Maintenance funds to service the contract are 
required to be budgeted by the State/UT Governments and placed at 
the disposal of the State Rural Roads Development Agencies 
(SRRDAs) in a separate account. The routine inspections on roads are 
conducted on a bi-monthly basis and the expenditure is based on the 
performance. On expiry of the 5 years, during the post Defect Liability 
Period (post DLP), the roads are placed under Zonal maintenance 
contracts for a further term of 5 years, which includes renewal and 
maintenance from time to time. The budget for the same is also 
allocated by the State/UT governments. 
 
(d):  The details of funds allocated, released and utilised under 
PMGSY during the last five years is given at Annexure.  
  
(e):  Ministry of Rural Development has taken a number of initiatives 
to expedite completion of road works sanctioned under PMGSY: 
(i)  PMGSY has a robust mechanism in place to ensure effective 
monitoring and quality construction of works. To effectively monitor 
the scheme and bring about greater efficiency, accountability and 
transparency in implementation, a modern web-based Online 
Management, Monitoring, and Accounting System (OMMAS) has been 
set up for PMGSY. Implementation of all sanctioned works is being 
monitored through OMMAS on a real-time basis to ensure that the 
physical and financial progress are in sync with the overall targets 
given to states. Further, a Project Management Information System 

(PMIS) has been developed for better management of the 
construction activities of each road sanctioned under PMGSY-III. 
(ii)  To enhance transparency during road construction, it has been 
made mandatory to install Global Positioning System (GPS) enabled 
Vehicle Tracking System (VTS) on all vehicles/machinery/equipment 
deployed by the contractor/PIUs for execution of PMGSY works. This 
helps in assessing the proper operation of this machinery/equipment 
for a specified period, which is essential for achieving the specified 
quality of the roads being constructed.  
(iii)  Further, as a measure of further enhancing the focus on 
maintenance of roads during the defect liability period and also 
streamlining the delivery of routine maintenance of PMGSY roads, 
eMARG has been introduced, which is conceptualized on 
Performance Based Maintenance Contracts (PBMC). As mentioned in 
reply to (b) above, payment to the contractor is now made through 
eMARG, which is based on the condition of road, its cross drainage 
works and traffic assets. Payments are based on how well the 
contractor manages to comply with the performance standards or 
service levels defined in the contract. 
(iv)  Electronic Maintenance of PMGSY roads (e-MARG), an online 
platform, has been implemented in all the states/UTs to monitor 
maintenance of PMGSY works for five years from the date of 
completion (i.e. under Defect Liability Period- DLP). Consequent upon 
the introduction of e-MARG i.e. software module for maintenance 
payments to the contractor during the defect liability period, such 
payments have been made commensurate with the quality of roads 
through a performance-based contract management system. 
(v)  Programme is regularly monitored by way of Regional Review 
Meetings (RRMs), Performance Review Committee (PRC) meetings, 
monthly review meetings and Pre-Empowered/Empowered 
Committee meetings with the States/UTs. The State/UT Governments 
are also regularly advised to convene meetings with the concerned 
authorities to expedite matters relating to land issues, forest and 
wildlife clearances in order to expedite completion of works. 
(vi)  A recent initiative about provision of unique digital identity (QR 
code)  to every PMGSY road marks a transformative shift in how rural 
infrastructure is managed. Under the framework, each road will be 
assigned a geo-spatial identification number linked to a QR code. This 
identity will be displayed on roadside signboards and backed by a 

digital record containing its location, classification and assset 
details. In effect, every road becomes a traceable, searchable entity 
in a national inventory.  On scanning the QR code, the public can 
place the grievance through Meri Sadak mobile application as well as 
the CPGRAMS portal. All the complaints are redressed through digital 
systems in an accountable manner.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF FISHERIES, ANIMAL HUSBANDRY AND DAIRYING  
DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES 
 
 LOK SABHA 
 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO - 1580 
ANSWERED ON 28/07/2026 
 
DEVELOPMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUACULTURE INFRASTRUCTURE IN 
TAMIL NADU 
 
1580.  Shri Tharaniventhan M S: 
 
Will the Minister of FISHERIES, ANIMAL HUSBANDRY AND DAIRYING be pleased to 
state: 
 
(a)  the current status of fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure in the country including the 
number of harbours, landing centers , cold storage facilities and processing units in the country 
including Tamil Nadu;  
(b)  the funds allocated, released and utilized by the Government for the development of 
fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure including Arani Constituency of Tamil Nad u during the 
last five years;  
(c)  the steps taken by the Government to ensure that small -scale and artisanal fishermen in 
remote and coastal areas of Tamil Nadu have access to modern infrastructure, credit and 
technical support;  
(d)  the measures being implemented to promote sustainable fishing practices, increase fish 
production and improve market access for fish and aquaculture products in Tamil Nadu; and  
(e)  whether the Government plans to introduce any reforms, expansions or new schemes to 
further strengthen fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure in Tamil Nadu and if so, the details 
thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
 
THE MINISTER OF FISHERIES, ANIMAL HUSBANDRY AND DAIRYING 
(SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH ALIAS LALAN SINGH) 
 
(a): The Fisheries and Aquaculture Infrastructure facilities in the country includes 76 fishing 
harbours, 231 fish landing centre s, 670 processing units, 641 pre -processing units,  739 cold 
storages, 51 chilled storages, 82 dry fish storages and 47  other fish storage facilities. These 
infrastructure includes 15 fishing harbours, 44 fish landing centres in Tamil Nadu and further as 
per information received from MPEDA, 63 processing units, 54 pre -processing units, 67 cold 
storages, 15 chilled storages , 6 dry fish storages and 9 other fish storage facilities are located in 
Tamil Nadu.  
 
 

(b): The Department of Fisheries, Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying  
with effect from financial year 2020-21 has been implementing Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada 
Yojana (PMMSY) in all the States/UTs including Tamil Nadu for the holistic development of 
fisheries sector. The development of fisheries infrastructure facilities is one of the important area 
envisaged and are supported under the PMMSY.  In addition, the Department of Fisheries, 
Government of India with effect from financial year 2018 -19 is also implementing Fisheries and 
Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF) to create and strengthen fisheries and 
aquaculture infrastructure in the country. Under FIDF, the Department of Fisheries, Government 
of India provided inter est-subvention upto 3% on the loan availed by Eligible Entities including 
States/UTs for development of fisheries and aquaculture development facilities.  
 
 
The Department of Fisheries, Government of India during  the last five years has  accorded 
approvals to the fisheries development projects of  Government of Tamil Nadu at a total cost of 
Rs 1,166.37 crore with Central share of Rs  452.39 crore. Against this approved amount of 
Rs.208.38 crore as central share  has been released to the State Government under PMMSY. In 
addition, the Department of Fisheries, Government of India during the last five years has also 
approved fisheries infrastructure pr ojects at a total cost of Rs 1059.67 crore under FIDF in the 
State of Tamil Nadu. The Government of Tamil Nadu has reported that no projects relating to 
fishing harbour infrastructure, fish landing centres, cold storage facilities, or fish processing units 
have been undertaken in the Arani Assembly Constituency during the last five years.  
 
 
(c) & (d): The Department of Fisheries, Government of India has taken up several measures 
for the benefits of fishers and fish farmers  in the country including Tamil Nadu for facilitating 
seamless access to modern infrastructure facilities, institutional credit, promotion of sustainable 
fishing practises and improving market access including the key activities as mentioned below:  
 
(i) Support to the State  Governments and other entities under ongoing Schemes of 
PMMSY and FIDF for creation of need based fisheries and aquaculture infrastructure 
facilities   
(ii) Issuance of Kisan Credit Card (KCC) to the fishers and fish farmers for their working 
capital requirements 
(iii) Advising the State Government s from time to time for strict  implementation of the 
provisions of Marine Fishing Regulation Act (MFRA) for regulation of fishing 
activities including mesh-size regulations. 
(iv) Implementation of 61 days uniform ban on fishing in the Indian EEZ annually, 

(v) Ban on destructive fishing practices in the Indian EEZ viz. paired bottom trawling or 
bull trawling and use of artificial and LED lights in fishing, 
(vi) Declaration of marine protected areas (MPAs) and protection  of endangered, 
threatened and protected (ETP) species, 
(vii) Installation of Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) in trawl nets, fishing gear and 
minimum legal size (MLS) of fishes, spatial -temporal restrictions, zonation of fishing 
areas by the coastal States/UTs, 
(viii) Installation of artificial reefs and Fish Aggregating Devices. 
(ix) Support for alternative livelihood activities such as mariculture, cage culture, seaweed 
cultivation, ornamental fisheries, crab farming, pearl farming, bivalve cultivation etc.  
(x) Providing livelihood and nutritional support to fishers during the fishing ban period. 
(xi) Group Accidental Insurance scheme to fishers.  
(xii) Providing safety and communication devices, installation of transponders, to ensure 
safety and security of fishers while fishing at sea.  
(xiii) Support for acquisition of fishing boats and nets, deep sea- fishing vessels. 
(xiv) Training, skilling, capacity building to fishers and fish farmers.  
(xv) Notification of Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) Rules and High Sea guidelines to 
facilitate marine fishers for sustainable harnessing of untapped fisheries resources for 
their economic prosperity.  
(xvi) Stock enhancement programmes like sea ranching.  
(xvii) Development of fishermen villages as Climate Resilient Coastal Fishermen Villages.  
 
 (e) Since the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) and the Fisheries and 
Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF)  scheme are already applicable to all 
States/Union Territories, including Tamil Nadu,  the question of introducing a separate scheme 
exclusively for Tamil Nadu does not arise.

(a) whether the Government has assessed the impact of below-normal rainfall in June 2026 on

(b) the details of rainfall deficiency, the status of Kharif sowing, and districts affected by the 
delayed monsoon, with specific details regarding the situation in Sitapur, Uttar Pradesh State-
wise;   
(c) the special steps taken by the Government to provide timely irrigation water to farmers in case 
of low rainfall;   
(d) whether any special provisions for drought-resistant seeds, irrigation assistance, and crop 
insurance have been made for the affected areas, if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the Government's action plan to mitigate the adverse impact on farmers' income and

ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF STATE FOR AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE 
कृͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण राÏय मंğी (SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR)

estimates for all major Kharif crops in the 2026-27 agricultural year (July–June) have not yet been 
released. The Status of Kharif sowing as on 17.07.2026 is attached as Annexure – I. 
States and Districts wise rainfall in all States are available on Indian Meteorological

(c) & (d): The Central Water Commission and State Governments have been advised to undertake 
advance planning for optimum utilization of reservoir water and promote efficient irrigation 
practices. Assistance to farmers is available through ongoing schemes such as Pradhan Mantri 
Krishi Sinchayee Yojana: Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) with a focus on enhancing water-use 
efficiency at the farm level through installation of Micro-Irrigation systems. Department of Rural 
Development is utilising Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB 
G Ram G) funds for rejuvenating water structures – such as farm ponds, check dams, canal 
desilting, and bori bandhans – to trap every drop of early or residual rainfall. Further, as part of 
the climate resilient agricultural practices, the Department is also implementing various Schemes 
viz. the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), Kisan Credit Card (KCC), Mission for 
Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH), National Food Security Mission (NFSM), 
Integrated Scheme on Oilseeds Mission and other existing programmes across the country.  

A nationwide Khet Bachao Abhiyaan was organised during 1-30 June, 2026 in which 80,67300 
farmers participated in 1,14,567 programmes which were organised to promote water 
conservation, introduce efficient irrigation and climate-resilient farming practices. Simultaneously, 
an intensive Kisan Credit Card (KCC) saturation drive and awareness campaign under Pradhan 
Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is being implemented in the districts categorised as 
vulnerable in view of the rainfall situation as forecast by the IMD.  
DA&FW has issued an advisory to the states (including Uttar Pradesh) and U.T. 
Administration to support pre-season planning for district level crop and variety selection, State 
level seed reserve of early maturing- short duration varieties under the National Seed Reserve 
(NSR) framework, activation of contingency seed reserves before monsoon onset and seed 
quality and quantity monitoring during peak demand. 
For the year 2026-27, an amount of 2684.72 Lakh has been approved under Annual Action 
Plan of Uttar Pradesh for the taking up the Interventions under National Food Security and 
Nutrition Mission (NFSNM): Seed components.  
(e): Government of India has substantially enhanced the Budget allocation of the Ministry of 
Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) from Rs. 27,622.67 crore (BE) during 2013-14 to Rs. 
1,40,416.57 crore (BE) during 2026-27.

Annexure-III  
Action plan to mitigate the adverse impact on farmers' income and agricultural production 
due to deficient rainfall 
 
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare is continuously monitoring the evolving 
monsoon situation and the possible impact of El Niño conditions on agriculture in close 
coordination with the India Meteorological Department (IMD), various Indian Council of Agriculture 
Research (ICAR) institutions, ICAR- Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture (CRIDA), 
Central Water Commission (CWC), Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), Mahalanobis National 
Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC), the Department of Food and Public Distribution (DFPD), the 
Department of Fertilisers (DoF) and State Governments. 
District Agriculture Contingency Plans (DACPs) have been updated for 14 States covering 
342 Districts which have been forecast to receive below normal rainfall by the ICAR Central 
Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture (ICAR-CRIDA) in consultation with the States for 
implementation.  
Interface meetings by ICAR have been conducted with 14 States, including Maharashtra, 
for operationalization of District Agriculture Contingency Plans (DACPs). Standard Operating 
Procedures (SOPs) have also been issued by ICAR for Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) for 
mitigation of El Niño-related risks.  
  Adequate availability of seeds has been ensured, against the demand of 172.80 lakh 
quintals from the States, there was availability of 192.25 lakh quintals of Kharif crop seeds. States 
have maintained 1% seeds i.e. 1.74 Lakh quintals as National Seed Reserve.  
Special emphasis has been laid on promoting crop diversification, promotion of short-
duration and drought-tolerant crop varieties, balanced use of fertilizers, water conservation 
practices, micro-irrigation, mulching, inter-cropping and practices of other climate-resilient 
technologies. Due to the delay in monsoon as well as the adverse impact of El Nino conditions, 
sowing is likely to be affected in respect of Tur, Soybean and Cotton and accordingly, the 
advisories to the farmers have been given to sow Maize, Bajra and Moong, and other short 
duration crops.  
In addition, as per the National Policy on Disaster Management (NPDM), the State 
Government is primarily responsible for providing necessary relief measures at the ground level 
in the wake of notified calamities. The State Governments undertake relief measures in the wake 
of natural calamities from funds available in the form of the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) 
in accordance with the approved guidelines. Additional financial assistance, over and above 
SDRF, is considered from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF), as per laid down 
procedure, in case of disaster of ‘severe nature’, which includes an assessment based on the visit 
of an Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT). The financial assistance provided under SDRF and 
NDRF is by way of relief and not for compensation of losses suffered/ claimed.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE 
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE 
 
LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 1582 
 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 28th JULY, 2026 
 
MODERN FARMING AND AGRO PROCESSING 
 
1582. SHRI RAJESH RANJAN: 
 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE कृͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण 
मंğी be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government has considered providing additional financial assistance 
to farmers for promoting natural farming, organic farming and drone-based agriculture; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Government has considered implementing any special scheme to 
promote maize, fox nut, jute and horticulture-based agro-processing industries in the 
Kosi-Seemanchal region of Bihar, including Purnia, Katihar, Araria, Kishanganj, 
Saharsa, Supaul and Madhepura; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF STATE FOR AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE  
कृͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण राÏय मंğी  (SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR) 
(a) & (b): The Government is promoting natural farming, organic farming and use 
of drone in agriculture through various ongoing schemes/programmes. The Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of National Mission on Natural Farming is being implemented 
since November, 2024 across the country to promote natural farming. The Mission 
facilitates adoption of natural farming through formation of clusters, capacity building 
of community resource persons (Krishi Sakhis), establishment of Bio-Input Resource 
Centers and farmer training and awareness programmes. The Mission provides output 
based incentive of ₹4000/- per acre, per year to a farmer for 2 years (up to 1 acre per 
farmer).  
  

 
     Organic farming is being promoted under the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana 
(PKVY) of PM-RKVY and Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North 
Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) for the North Eastern States. Under PKVY, an 
assistance of Rs. 31,500 per ha is provided over 3 years for promotion of organic 
farming. Under MOVCDNER, an assistance of Rs. 46,500/ha is provided over 3 years 
for creation of Farmers Producer Organization, to support to farmers for organic inputs 
etc. Both schemes stress on end-to-end support to farmers engaged in organic 
farming i.e. from production to processing, certification and marketing. Primary focus 
of the schemes is to form organic clusters, with preference to small and marginal 
farmers, to create a supply chain.  
 
    The Government is also promoting the use of drones in agriculture under the Sub-
mission on Agriculture Mechanization (SMAM).  Under the scheme, financial 
assistance @ 100% of the cost of drone up to a maximum of Rs. 10 lakhs per drone 
is provided for its purchase and demonstration on the farmers’ fields by the institutes 
under Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Farm Machinery Training & 
Testing Institutes, Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), State Agriculture Universities 
(SAUs), State and other Central Government Agricultural Institutions/Departments 
and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) of Government of India engaged in agricultural 
activities. The Farmers Producers Organizations (FPOs) are provided grants up to 
75% of the cost of Kisan Drone for its demonstrations on the farmers’ fields. In order 
to make available drone services to farmers on rental basis, financial assistance @ 
40% up to a maximum of Rs. 4.00 lakhs are provided for purchase of drones by CHCs 
under Cooperative Society of Farmers, FPOs and Rural entrepreneurs. Agriculture 
graduates establishing CHCs are eligible to receive financial assistance @ 50% of the 
cost of drone up to a maximum of Rs.5.00 lakhs per drone. For purchase of drones on 
individual ownership basis, the Small and Marginal, Scheduled Caste/Scheduled 
Tribe, Women and North Eastern State farmers are provided financial assistance @ 
50% of the cost up to a maximum of Rs. 5.00 lakhs and other farmers @ 40% up to a 
maximum of Rs. 4.00 lakhs per drone. 
  

     In addition, the Central Sector Scheme of Namo Drone Didi is being implemented 
in convergence with other ongoing schemes. The objective of the scheme is to 
promote advance technology in agriculture for improving efficiency, enhancing crop 
yield and reducing cost of operation and to empower Women Self Help Groups (SHGs) 
as drone service providers for increasing their income and providing livelihood support 
to them. 
(c) & (d):  The Government is implementing various schemes to promote maize, 
fox nut (makhana), jute, and horticulture-based agro-processing industries across the 
country, including in Bihar's Kosi-Seemanchal region, covering the districts of Purnia, 
Katihar, Araria, Kishanganj, Saharsa, Supaul, and Madhepura. 
     Production of Maize and Jute are being promoted under the National Food Security 
and Nutrition Mission (NFSNM) through interventions such as distribution of quality 
seeds, demonstration of improved production technologies and capacity building of 
farmers. Horticulture crops are promoted under the Mission for Integrated 
Development of Horticulture (MIDH), which provides assistance for area expansion, 
quality planting material, protected cultivation, post-harvest management and value 
addition. Assistance is also extended for establishment of infrastructure relating to 
integrated cold chain supply system, refrigerated vans/containers, primary/mobile 
processing units, ripening chambers, evaporative/low energy cool chambers, 
preservation units etc. under Integrated Post Harvest Management component of 
MIDH. 
    To support the promotion of Foxnut (Makhana), the Central Sector Scheme for 
Development of Makhana has been launched for the period 2025–26 to 2030–31. The 
scheme aims at the holistic development of the makhana (foxnut) sector by addressing 
key components such as production and productivity enhancement, post-harvest 
management, value addition, research and development, marketing, branding, export 
promotion, and capacity building. The scheme is being implemented by the National 
Makhana Board in close coordination with the State Governments, including the 
Government of Bihar. Under the scheme, financial assistance is provided for the 
establishment of micro, small, medium, and large makhana processing units for 
processing raw makhana into popped makhana and for undertaking further value 
addition. Credit-linked back-ended subsidy is admissible at the rate of 35% for private 
sector entrepreneurs and 50% for Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs). 

      Support for post-harvest infrastructure and agro-processing is also available under 
the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF). Further, the Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries (MoFPI) is promoting the overall development of the food-processing 
sector, including rural areas, through its flagship schemes namely the Pradhan Mantri 
Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY), the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Food 
Processing Industry (PLISFPI) and the Centrally Sponsored Pradhan Mantri 
Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME) Scheme. Assistance 
under these schemes is available to eligible beneficiaries across the country, including 
Bihar, as per the respective scheme guidelines. 
      Under MoFPI, the details of the projects sanctioned and scheme implementation 
in the Kosi-Seemanchal region of Bihar, including Purnia, Katihar, Araria, Kishanganj, 
Saharsa, Supaul, and Madhepura districts—are placed at Annexure I.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 1584 
 
TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 28TH JULY, 2026/ SHRAVANA 6, 1948 (SAKA) 
 
INCLUSION OF BHOJPURI LANGUAGE IN EIGHTH SCHEDULE 
 
†1584.      SHRI RAMASHANKAR VIDHARTHI RAJBHAR: 
 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government proposed contemplate on the proposal to 
include Bhojpuri language in the Eighth schedule of the Constitution; 
 
(b) if  so, the present status of the said proposal and the time by which 
Bhojpuri language is likely to be included in the Eighth schedule; and 
 
(c) if not, the reason therefor? 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI NITYANAND RAI) 
 
(a) to (c): There have been demands from time to time for inclusion of several 
languages, including Bhojpuri , in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution. 
However, there are no fixed criteria for consideration of any language for 
inclusion in the Eighth Schedul e to the Constitution. As the evolution of 
dialects and languages is a dynamic process, influenced by socio -cultural, 
economic and political developments, it is difficult to fix any criterion for 
languages for inclusion in the Eighth Schedule to the Consti tution. The  
earlier     attempts,      through     the      Pahwa     (1996)      and      Sitakant 
 

-2- 
L.S.US.Q.NO. 1584 FOR 28.07.2026  
Mohapatra (2003) Committees, to evolve such fixed criteria have been 
inconclusive. The Government is conscious of the sentiments and 
requirements for inclusion of other languages in the Eighth Schedule. Such 
requests have to be considered keeping in mind these sent iments, and the 
other relevant considerations. Since at present, there are no fixed criteria 
for any language to be considered for inclusion in the Eighth Schedule to the 
Constitution, no time -frame can be fixed for consideration of the demands 
for inclusion of more languages in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE & INDUSTRY 
DEPARTMENT FOR PROMOTION OF INDUSTRY AND INTERNAL TRADE

      TO BE ANSWERED ON TUESDAY, THE 28TH JULY, 2026. 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE SCHEME FOR STARTUPS 
 
1586.  DR. AMOL RAMSING KOLHE: 
 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
वाणिज्य  एवं उद्योग मंत्री 
(a)  whether Government has reviewed the implementation of the Credit Guarantee 
Scheme for Startups (CGSS) in Maharashtra, particularly in Pune, and if so, the 
details thereof; 
 
(b)  the number of Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) 
recognized start-ups in Maharashtra that have availed collateral -free credit 
under the Scheme during the last three years and the current year, along with 
amount of guarantee cover provided in Maharashtra,  district-wise including 
Pune; 
 
(c)  whether Government has assessed the reasons for the relatively low uptake of 
CGSS among eligible startups in  Pune, despite its large innovation and 
technology ecosystem, if so, the details thereof; 
 
(d)  whether any review has been undertaken regarding the participation of banks 
and member institutions in extending credit under the Scheme in Maharashtra, 
district-wise including Pune; and 
 
(e)  the measures taken by the Government to improve awareness, simplify 
procedures and enhance credit flow to DPIIT-recognized startups in Pune and 
other parts of Maharashtra? 
 
ANSWER 
 
वाणिज्य  एवं उद्योग मंत्रालय में राज्य मंत्री (श्री णिणिन प्रसाद)   
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE & INDUSTRY 
(SHRI JITIN PRASADA) 
 
(a) to (c): The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS) is implemented for 
enabling debt funding to startups through eligible financial institutions [Member 
Institutions (MIs)]. CGSS is operationalized by the National Credit Guarantee 
Trustee Company (NCGTC) Limit ed and has been operationalized from 1st 
April 2023. The CGSS is implemented across the country, including in the State 
of Maharashtra. 

Specifically in the State of Maharashtra, 118 loans amounting to around Rs 
326.07 crore have been guaranteed to startup borrowers under CGSS during 
the last three years and the current year viz. 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026 as on 
30th June 2026. Particularly in the district of Pune, 61 loans amounting to 
around Rs 149.87 crore have been guaranteed to startup borrowers under 
CGSS. The district -wise details for the State of Maharashtra are placed at 
Annexure-I. 
The Management Committee (MC) constituted under the Scheme is 
responsible for reviewing, supervising and monitoring the functioning of the 
Scheme and is empowered to appr aise its performance. Further, the MIs 
evaluate credit proposals based on prudent banking judgement and undertake 
due diligence while sanctioning and monitoring loans in accordance with the 
operational guidelines of the Scheme. The Scheme guidelines are av ailable 
online: 
https://www.ncgtc.in//content/products/0/20250509/Gazette_Notification_CGSS
_8th _May_2025_44e1a2d0dc.pdf 
(d) to (e): The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) and 
NCGTC engage with startups and Member Institutions (MIs) to review the 
implementation of the Scheme, address operational issues, discuss progress 
and facilitate greater participation o f lenders and uptake of the Scheme. In 
addition, the Management Committee also reviews the functioning and 
performance of the Scheme. 
Based on stakeholder discussions and fe edback, the Government expanded 
the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS) vide notification dated 8 th  
May 2025 by increasing the ceiling on guarantee cover per borrower from Rs. 
10 crore to Rs. 20 crore, enhancing guarantee coverage to 85% of the amount 
in default for loans up to Rs. 10 crore and 75% for loans above Rs. 10 crore, as 
well as reducing the Annual Guarantee Fee (AGF) to 1% for lenders supporting 
startups in 27 Champion Sectors, and introducing operational reforms for wider 
coverage of eligible startups. 
The Government has also undertaken several measures to improve 
awareness, simplify access and enhance credit flow to startups across the 
country, including in the State of Maharashtra: 
i. Launch of the Startup Common Application Journey on the Jan Samarth 
Portal, providing a unified digital platform for startups to apply fo r loans 
and track their application. 
ii. Organization of awareness and outreach programmes by DPIIT in 
collaboration with NCGTC across various cities, including Mumbai, 
bringing together startups and MIs to improve awareness and facilitate 
access to credit 
iii. Regular interactions with the leadership of MIs to address implementation 
issues, review progress and facilitate improved credit flow under the 
Scheme. 
 

As a result of such initiatives, the number and value of guarantees under the 
Scheme have witnessed notabl e growth. As on 30th June 2026, 478 loans 
amounting to approximately Rs. 1,469.92 crore have been guaranteed under 
the Scheme, of which more than Rs. 660 crore has been guaranteed during 
2026 (up to 30th June 2026).

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
DEPARTMENT OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 1587 
  ANSWERED ON 28/07/2026 
 
LAUNCHING OF VB-G RAM-G SCHEME 
 
1587. Shri Subbarayan K: 
 Com. Selvaraj V: 
 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rojgar 
and Aajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM-G) Scheme introduced 
in place of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment 
Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) has come into force from July 
1st, 2026; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof; 
(c)  whether the attention of the Government has been drawn to the 
protest actions against the replacement of MGNREGS by a new 
scheme by various organisations; and 
(d)  if so, the details of the concerns expressed by these 
organisations against the new scheme and demanding the 
restoration of the old scheme and the reaction of the 
Government? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI KAMLESH PASWAN) 
  
(a) & (b): The Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika 
Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G) Act, 2025 has come into force with 
effect from 1st July, 2026  in rural areas of the entire country. All 
States and Union Territories have notified Viksit Bharat G RAM G 
Scheme in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and have 
started implementing the same. 
  
(c) & (d): Certain expressions of views/concerns by some 
organisations in relation to the implementation of the VB–G RAM G 
Act have been reported in sections of the media. The concerns, inter 
alia, relate to the replacement of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, the continued demand-driven 

Page 2 of 2 
 
nature of the programme and the apprehension that a phase-wise 
implementation strategy may adversely affect employment 
opportunities for rural workers. 
  
In this regard, it is stated that the VB–G RAM G Act, 2025 
preserves the statutory, demand-driven nature of the rural 
employment guarantee by providing 125 days of guaranteed wage 
employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult 
members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. The Act further 
strengthens the programme by placing greater emphasis on 
sustainable livelihood creation, durable and productive rural assets, 
water security, climate resilience, transparency and technology-
enabled governance, while retaining the statutory right to demand 
employment and receive unemployment allowance in accordance 
with the provisions of the Act.  
  
Under VB G RAM G, from July 1st 2026, over 99.5% workers who 
demanded employment have been offered employment and 5.20 
Crore persondays have been generated across 8.46 lakh worksites as 
on 22.07.2026.

INCLUSION OF GINGER UNDER PMFBY 
1588. Shri Shreyas M Patel: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE कृ ͪष एवं ͩकसान 
कãयाण मंğी be pleased to state:  
 (a) whether Ginger is presently covered under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima 
Yojana (PMFBY) in all States and Union Territories, including Karnataka; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons for its exclusion in certain States 
or districts; 
(c) whether the Government has received representations from the Government of 
Karnataka, farmers organisations or public representatives seeking inclusion of 
Ginger under PMFBY; 
(d) whether the Government has assessed the losses suffered by Ginger growers 
due to diseases, pests, excessive rainfall, drought, floods and market-related risks; 
(e) whether the Government proposes to include Ginger as an insured crop under 
PMFBY in Karnataka and other Ginger-growing regions or provide a suitable crop 
insurance package for Ginger farmers; and 
(f) if so, the details and expected timeline and if not, the reasons therefor ? 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE FOR AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE  
कृ ͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण राÏय मंğी   (SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR) 
(a) to  (c):  The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) envisages coverage of 
all food crops  (cereals, millets and pulses), oilseeds and commercial/horticultural 
crops subject to availability of past yield data based on Crop Cutting Experiments  
(CCEs)  as well as capacity of the State Government to conduct requisite number of 
CCEs or adopt YES-TECH (Yield Estimation System Based on Technology) to 
assess the yield of the crop to calculate claims. 

     For the crops not meeting the aforesaid conditions, the concerned State 
Government is free to notify them for coverage under Restructured Weather Based 
Crop Insurance Scheme  (RWBCIS)  under which claims payment are being 
structured on the basis of weather index parameters. 
However, specific crop is notified by the concerned State Government 
keeping in view the afore-said provision. Accordingly, Ginger has been notified by 
the State government of Karnataka in the districts of Bidar, Haveri, Shivamogga and 
Uttara Kannada in Karnataka from Kharif 2020-21 onwards. Ginger is also notified in 
States of Chhattisgarh, Kerala, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Odisha, Sikkim,  Tamil Nadu 
and Uttarakhand during 2025-26. 
 
(d): The RWBCIS is being implemented on weather index-based approach, under 
which insurance claims are determined solely on the basis of deviations in the 
notified weather parameters like deficit and excess rainfall, high or low temperature, 
humidity etc., which are deemed to impact crop production adversely and recorded 
at the designated Reference and Backup Weather Stations, as specified in the 
approved Term Sheets. Market-related risks are not covered under the Scheme. 
 
(e) & (f):  The notification of a specific crop is the prerogative of the State 
Government and State Government has accordingly notified Ginger under the 
scheme as stated above.

COMPENSATION TO CHILLI GROWERS 
 
1589. Shri G Kumar Naik: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE 
 कृ िष एवं िकसान कÐयाण मंýी  be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government has assessed extent of crop damage and yield losses caused by black thrips and other 
emerging pests in chilli-growing areas of Raichur district and other parts of Karnataka and if so, the details thereof; 
(b) whether the Government has conducted any assessment of the impact of erratic monsoon patterns, water stress 
and rising temperatures on chilli cultivation in Raichur and the measures taken to promote climate-resilient 
cultivation practices and integrated pest management; 
(c) whether the Government has assessed the increase in the cost of chilli cultivation and the extent of 
indebtedness among chilli farmers in Raichur and if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether the Government proposes to provide any special assistance, compensation or crop protection package 
for chilli growers affected by pest attacks and climatic stress; and 
(e) the measures taken or proposed to stabilise chilli prices and protect farmers from severe market fluctuations? 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE 
कृ िष एवं िकसान कÐयाण राºय मंýी (SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR) 
(a): Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (ICAR-IIHR), Bengaluru, 
along with other ICAR Institutes and State Agricultural Universities, has conducted survey during the year 2021 
on thrips incidence in chilli-growing areas of Karnataka. Only a small proportion of Thrips hawaiiensis, T. florum, 
and T. palmi were observed on chilli during the survey period. The dominant thrips species recorded in Raichur 
during 2021 was Thrips parvispinus, accounting for 94–96% of the total thrips population, followed by T. 
hawaiiensis (3%), T. florum (1%), and T. palmi (<1%). Thus, T. parvispinus was identified as the predominant 
thrips species infesting chilli. Based on these findings, various remedial measures, including a management 
schedule for controlling thrips in chilli, were recommended. The current chilli crop is largely at the nursery stage 

and no major incidence of black thrips or other emerging pests has been reported so far during the present season 
in Raichur district. 
(b): ICAR-IIHR, Bengaluru has recommended drought and heat-tolerant varieties/hybrids such as Arka Gagan, 
Arka Tejasvi and Arka Saanvi with climate-resilient cultivation practices including drip irrigation, mulching, 
balanced nutrient management and Integrated Pest Management (IPM). State Government has also advised to 
adopt climate-resilient cultivation practices including the selection of suitable short-duration and climate-resilient 
chilli varieties such as Krishnaprabha-Rudra and to consider alternative short-duration crops wherever necessary.  
(c): The State Horticulture Department, Karnataka is aware of the increase in the cost of chilli cultivation due to 
the rising prices of seeds/seedlings, fertilizers, pesticides, labour, irrigation, machinery and other agricultural 
inputs. In this regard, while determining the Scale of Finance (SoF) for the year 2026–27, the increased cost of 
cultivation and various input costs were taken into consideration. Accordingly, the Scale of Finance recommended 
for chilli cultivation was increased from ₹ 55,884 per acre to ₹ 69,189 per acre. However, specific data regarding 
the extent of indebtedness among chilli farmers in Raichur district is not available with the State Horticulture 
Department. 
(d): The Government has been implementing the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) and the 
Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) to provide financial support to farmers suffering 
crop loss or damage arising out of natural calamities and adverse weather events. Under PMFBY Government of 
Karnataka has notified chilli as an insured crop under PMFBY/ RWBCIS. 
Assistance for Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in horticultural crops including chilli, is available 
under the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) @ 30% assistance, with a cost norm of 
₹5,000 per hectare for an area of up to 2 hectares per beneficiary.  
The State Governments undertake relief measures in the wake of natural disasters including pest attack 
from the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF), already placed at their disposal, in accordance with Government 
of India’s approved items and norms. In order to supplement the efforts of the State, additional financial assistance 
is extended from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF), in case of disaster of ‘severe nature’, in 
accordance with the established procedure. The financial assistance provided under SDRF and NDRF is by way 
of relief and not for compensation of loss suffered/ claimed. 
(e): To stabilise chilli prices and reduce post-harvest losses, assistance is available under the Mission for 
Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) for creation of post-harvest infrastructure including cold storage 
facilities. These interventions help to reduce post-harvest losses, minimise distress sales and enable farmers to 
realise better prices. 

Government is also implementing Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) Scheme to provide medium- and 
long-term debt financing for developing post-harvest management infrastructure. 1739 units for post-harvest 
storage structures (Cold Stores and Cold Chain, Silos and Warehouse) have been sanctioned under AIF in 
Karnataka. 
Further, to ensure remunerative prices for farmers producing perishable agricultural and horticultural 
commodities not covered under the Minimum Support Price (MSP) regime, the Government implements the 
Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) under the Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA). 
The Scheme is intended to protect farmers from distress sales during periods of bumper production when market 
prices fall below economic levels and the cost of production. MIS is implemented at the request of the concerned 
State/UT Government, subject to the prescribed guidelines including a decline of at least 10% in the prevailing 
market price compared to the previous normal year. The loss incurred under the Scheme is shared between the 
Central and State Governments in the ratio of 50:50 (75:25 for North-Eastern States). A new component of Price 
Differential Payment (PDP) with an option to make direct payment of the price difference between the Market 
Intervention Price (MIP) and the selling price to the farmers for the crops traded in the notified APMC Mandis 
has also been added to the Scheme. During 2025-26, MIP of Rs. 105,892.00 per Metric Tonnes with a sanction 
quantity of 73,732 Metric Tonnes was sanctioned to Karnataka. However, it could not be implemented due to 
prevailing market price above MIP.

1591. Shri Arun Kumar Sagar: 
 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 
(a)  whether the Central Government has identified roads under the 
priority to the most Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) 
by giving priority to the most backward areas within the 
Shahjahanpur Lok Sabha Constituency in the State of Uttar 
Pradesh; 
(b)  if so, the details thereof along with the names of those identified 
roads; and 
(c)  the time by which the construction of roads is proposed to be 
undertaken? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI KAMLESH PASWAN)  
(a): The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched 
as a one-time special intervention to provide single all-weather road 
connectivity to eligible unconnected habitations of designated 
population sizes, thereby, uplifting the socio-economic conditions of 
rural population in backward and remote areas. 
To ensure prioritized coverage of backward, tribal, and socio-
economically vulnerable communities, the Government has built 
specific relaxations and targeted interventions across various 
phases of the scheme: 
1. Special Population Relaxations under PMGSY-IV: 
The Union Cabinet approved Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana-
IV (PMGSY-IV), for implementation during FY 2024–25 to FY 2028–29 
with the target to provide all-weather road connectivity (construction 

Page 2 of 3 
 
of 62,500 km of roads) to 25,000 eligible unconnected habitations 
across the country with a total outlay of Rs.70,125 crore. There is no 
separate state-wise target under PMGSY-IV. The eligibility criteria of 
the habitations to be provided connectivity under PMGSY-IV based on 
population norms of Census 2011 are as follows: 
i. Habitations with a population of 500 and above in plains, 
ii. Habitations with a population of 250 and above in Special 
Category States (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Ladakh, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, 
Himachal Pradesh, Jammu Kashmir and Uttarakhand), 
Special Category Areas [Tribal Schedule-V Areas, Desert 
Areas, Aspirational Blocks/ Districts and Hilly areas as 
notified by the respective State Government (cross slope 
more than 25% gradient and the elevation is more than 
600 metres from the Mean Sea Level)] and 
iii. Habitations with a population of 100 and above in LWE 
affected Districts including Legacy & Thrust Districts 
identified by MHA from time to time. 
Under PMGSY-IV, a "Cluster Approach" has been introduced for 
habitations. This allows grouping smaller, isolated habitations within 
a radius of 500 meter (in plains) to collectively meet the population 
criteria, ensuring backward habitations are connected to essential 
services like schools, health centers, and agricultural markets. 
2. Targeted Interventions & Convergence Schemes: 
i. Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DA-JGUA): 
Integrated with PMGSY-IV to give priority connectivity to 
habitations having a population of 500+ with 50% or more 
Scheduled Tribe (ST) population, or habitations with 50+ 
ST population in Aspirational Districts. 
ii. Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana (PM-
AJAY): Integrated with PMGSY-IV to prioritize habitations 
having a population of 500+ with 40% or more Scheduled 
Caste (SC) population. 
iii. PM-JANMAN (Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha 
Abhiyan): A dedicated vertical launched to provide all-
weather road connectivity to ultra-vulnerable 
communities, specifically Particularly Vulnerable Tribal 
Groups (PVTGs), relaxing population norms down to 100+ 
(or clusters of 100+) based on Census 2011 survey data. 
In the Shahjahanpur Lok Sabha Constituency of Uttar Pradesh, all 
eligible habitations identified under various phases of PMGSY have 

Page 3 of 3 
 
been considered in accordance with these program guidelines. As per 
data available on the Online Management, Monitoring and Accounting 
System (OMMAS) as on 23.07.2026, a total of 91 roads of length 364 
km have been sanctioned in Shahjahanpur Lok Sabha Constitency 
since inception.

European Union (EU), and Japan, during the period 2018-2026* are given as Annexure 
I. The total number of rejection along with the estimated value of rejected containers is 
given in Annexure-II. 
(c) & (d)   The consignments rejected for parameters other t han antibiotic residues are 
permitted to be reprocessed and re -exported by Export Inspection Council (EIC) 
through its Exports Inspection Agencies (EIAs) which issues permission for re -export if 
the food safety parameters are found to comply with the natio nal regulations. 

2 
 
Permission for local sale is obtained from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of 
India (FSSAI) after the necessary testing is carried out by FSSAI-approved laboratories.  
(e)  The year -wise estimated financial loss incurred due to rej ections on account of 
antibiotic residues is enclosed as Annexure II . The major measures taken by the 
Government to address these concerns are given as follows: 
I. Policy Reforms for antibiotic bans: Government has notified various regulations 
in 2025 to comply with national and international standards on aquaculture 
products, which includes: 
i. S.O. 1158 (E) dated 12.03.2025 for prohibiting the import, manufacture, 
distribution, and sale of Chloramphenicol and Nitrofuran for use in any 
food-producing animal rearing system in India,  
ii. S.O. 1981 (E) dated 01.05.2025 amending S.O. 729 (E) to prohibit the use 
of 37 anti-microbials (reserved for human use) at any stage of aquaculture 
activities related to shrimp, prawn, fish and fishery products,  
iii. S.O. 4338(E) dated 23.09.2025 for prohibiting the import, manufacture, 
sale, and distribution of 34 listed anti-microbial medicinal products for 
veterinary use.  
II. Capacity building of shrimp farmers and processing workers including antibiotic 
awareness, Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) training, hygiene training, HACCP 
(Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) training;  
III. Notifying the registration of dealers to bring them under the regulatory regime;  
IV. Implementation of National Residue Control Programme and Pre-Harvest Testing 
to monitor residues and ensure antibiotic -reside free aquaculture shrimp 
production for export;  
V. Formulation of the National Framework for Traceability Systems in fisheries and 
aquaculture, etc.   
VI. Implementation of a nationwide app -based enrolment mechanism named “Aqua 
Trace” for aquaculture farms and hatcheries aimed at establishing a r obust 
traceability system and strengthening compliance with international food safety 
and sustainability standards.

WELFARE FOR DIVYANGJANS 
 
1594. Dr. Ganapathy Rajkumar P:  
Thiru Thanga Tamilselvan:  
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Union Government has any proposal to set up a Commission exclusively/solely 
for the welfare of divyangjans;  
(b) if so, the details thereof;  
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and  
(d) the timeline for such proposal considered in future? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE FOR SOCIAL JUSTICE & EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRI B L VERMA) 
 
(a) to (d): No. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016  provides a statutory 
institutional framework for the protection of the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities 
through the Office of the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (CCPD) at the 
Central level and the State Commissioners at the State level. The Office of the CCPD is 
empowered, inter alia, to review the safeguards available to persons with disabilities, monitor 
the implementation of the provisions of the Act, and recommend measures for the effective 
implementation of policies, programmes, schemes and projects. Further, the Central Advisory 
Board on Disability (CABD), constituted under the RPwD Act, 2016, facilitates coordination 
between the Central Government and the State Governments/UT Administrations and advises 
on policies, programmes, legislation and measures for the empowerment of persons with 
disabilities.

1595. SMT. DHANORKAR PRATIBHA SURESH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE कृ ͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण 
मंğी be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the Government has official data available regarding the fact that private 
insurance companies operating under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana 
(PMFBY) have earned substantial profits of rupees 73,630 crore from across the 
country and rupees 16,300 crore from Maharashtra alone during the last nine years 
(2016 to 2025); 
(b) whether the Government is considering imposing 'profit capping' on insurance 
companies to curb this profiteering, given that these companies often cite technical 
glitches and complex rules to reject farmers' claims or provide only nominal assistance 
during natural disasters; 
(c) the details of the reforms being made in the regulations to make it mandatory for 
insurance companies to conduct 'panchnama' (spot assessment) within 72 hours of 
crop loss and deposit the claim amount directly into farmers' bank accounts within the 
next 15 days; and 
(d) the stringent steps being taken to the Government to cancel the licenses of 
companies violating the terms and to register criminal cases against them ? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE FOR AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE  
कृ ͪष एवं ͩकसान कãयाण राÏय मंğी  (SHRI RAMNATH THAKUR) 
(a):   All the data relating to coverage  details including premium and claims relating to 
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is available on National Crop Insurance 
Portal (NCIP). This data includes the premia paid as well as the claims disbursed. 
Data regarding profit and/or loss of insurance companies is not maintained on the 
portal. 
(b): No such proposal is under consideration. However, an Alternate Risk Transfer 
Mechanism (ARTM) has been introduced from Kharif 2023. ARTM provides for 3 
Alternate Risk Transfer models other than standard PMFBY namely, cup and cap 
model (80:110), cup and cap model (60:130) and profit and loss sharing model under 
which in case of claims below stipulated threshold, portion of the premium paid by the 
Government as subsidy will go back to the State treasury or Consolidated Fund of 
India, as the case may be.   Further, in case of claims above stipulated threshold, 
Centre and State are required to pay claims.    
  

(c) & (d): Timelines have already been fixed for each and every activity including 
conduct of survey in case of localized calamities and settlement of claims in farmers 
account and season-end area approach based claims and has been duly provided in 
the Operational Guidelines of the scheme.     
 
Further, Crop Loss Assessment App (CLAP), developed as a digital mobile 
application to streamline and improve the efficiency of crop loss assessments for 
localised calamities/ post harvest losses for individual farms and land parcels under 
PMFBY.  The use of CLAP has been made mandatory for all the States/UTs under the 
scheme.  In case of localized calamities, a duly filled & signed copy of survey form is 
given to the insured farmer by the surveyor of insurance company.  
To bring more transparency in calculation of claims, results of CCEs are required 
to be uploaded on the National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP).  Further, the insurance 
companies have also been instructed to witness the conduct of CCEs.    As per 
provisions of the CCEs manual under PMFBY, results of the CCEs done through CCE 
Agri App, are required to be noted on the prescribed form with the signature of the 
concerned officers conducting the CCEs, farmers and officers of insurance companies 
witnessing the CCEs. 
 
As per timelines given in the Operational Guidelines of the scheme, insurance 
companies have to settle the claims within 21 Days from calculation of claims on 
National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP) subject to receipt of premium subsidy.   In case 
payment is not made as per timelines mentioned above penalty of 12% is auto 
calculated and levied through NCIP w.e.f. Kharif 2024 season.

PENDING ROAD PROJECTS UNDER PMGSY 
 
1597. Dr. Prashant Yadaorao Padole: 
 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 
(a)  whether the Government is aware that Bhandara and Gondia 
districts are Naxal-affected and predominantly tribal districts 
where road connectivity is vital for development, security, 
education, healthcare and rural livelihoods, if so, the details 
thereof; 
(b)  whether adequate funds have not been provided for several road 
projects in these districts under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak 
Yojana (PMGSY) during the last four years, resulting in delays in 
construction, maintenance and deterioration of road conditions; 
(c)  if so, the details of funds sanctioned, released and utilized under 
PMGSY for Bhandara and Gondia districts during the last four 
years, year-wise; 
(d)  whether poor road conditions are causing serious hardships to 
villagers, students, farmers, patients and security forces in 
these areas, if so, the details thereof; and 
(e)  whether the Government proposes to provide special financial 
assistance and prepare a time-bound action plan for completion 
of all pending and proposed road projects in Bhandara and 
Gondia districts, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons 
therefor? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI KAMLESH PASWAN)  
  
(a) to (e):  Under PMGSY, special emphasis is accorded for improving 
rural road connectivity in Aspirational Districts, tribal areas, Left 
Wing Extremism (LWE)-affected areas and other remote and difficult 
regions, in accordance with the scheme guidelines and approved 
framework in order to promote socio-economic development, 

Page 2 of 3 
 
improving access to education, healthcare and agricultural markets, 
and facilitating rural livelihoods. Accordingly, the Government has 
adopted the following mechanisms to prioritize road connectivity in 
such areas: 
(i)  Priority to eligible unconnected habitations located in 
Aspirational Districts, tribal and remote areas while preparing 
proposals under the relevant verticals of PMGSY, subject to eligibility 
under the scheme by identifying such projects under Comprehensive 
New Connectivity Priority List (CNCPL). The sanctions and 
implementation of projects are done as per the CNCPL list.  
(ii)  Dedicated interventions such as the Road Connectivity Project 
for Left Wing Extremism Affected Areas (RCPLWEA) to improve 
connectivity in LWE-affected districts. 
(iii)  Under PMGSY-IV unconnected habitations of population size 
(as per Census 2011) 500+ in plains, 250+ in Special Category States 
(Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Ladakh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu Kashmir and 
Uttarakhand), Special Category Areas [(Tribal Schedule-V Areas, 
Desert Areas, Aspirational Blocks/ Districts and Hilly areas as notified 
by the respective State Government (cross slope more than 25% 
gradient and the elevation is more than 600 meters from the Mean 
Sea Level)] and 100+ in LWE affected Districts including Legacy & 
Thrust Districts identified by MHA from time to time.  
(iv)  Under PMGSY-IV, habitations identified under Vibrant Village 
Program-II are being prioritised for all-weather road connectivity. 
(v)  Under PM-JANMAN, road connectivity is being provided to 
eligible Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG) habitations with 
a population of 100+, to improve access to essential services and 
socio-economic opportunities.   
In the district of Bhandara, since inception till date, a total of 
171 roads covering 717.47 km and 9 bridges have been sanctioned 
under various verticals of the PMGSY, out of which, 171 roads 
covering 710.90 km and 9 bridges have already been constructed. 
Similarly, in Gondia district, since inception till date, a total of 285 
road works covering 1,130.24 km and 16 bridges have been 
sanctioned. All the sanctioned road works and bridges have been 
completed. 

Page 3 of 3 
 
  
The funds for implementation of the schemes are released by the 
Ministry to the States/UTs as a whole and not district-wise. Further, 
the funds are released on the basis of works in hand, the progress 
achieved in the project and after due submission of necessary 
documents.  Currently, the fund releases under PMGSY are through 
the SNA SPARSH system. The funds released and expenditure 
incurred by the State of Maharashtra, during the last four years and 
current year, are as under: -

Under PMGSY-IV, the State Government has surveyed

(a) & (b): The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Ministry of Statistics and

(SAS) of Agricultural Households during NSS 77th round (January, 2019 – December,

agricultural household increased from ₹6,426 in 2012-13 (NSS 70th round) to ₹10,218 
in 2018-19 (NSS 77th round).

The details of the cost of cultivation of crops for which MSP is declared is 
available at https://cacp.da.gov.in. Farm Harvest Prices of Principal Crops in India is 
available at https://desagri.gov.in.  
Every year, the Government fixes Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for 22 
agricultural crops for the country as a whole, based on the recommendations of the 
Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP), and after considering the views 
of the State Governments and Central Ministries/Departments concerned. The policy 
ensures a minimum margin of 50 percent over the all-India weighted average cost of 
production. The crop-wise Minimum Support Price of crops and procurement data for 
the last five years are placed at Annexure I & II. 
(c): The Government has taken various measures to provide remunerative prices 
to the farmers for their agricultural produce. Minimum Support Price (MSP) for 22 
notified agricultural crops are fixed annually by the Government. Since 2014, farmers 
have received more than Rs. 27.80 lakh crore through MSP procurement of about 
12819 LMT of agricultural produce.  
 
Government procures cereals and coarse cereals through Food Corporation of 
India (FCI) and other designated State Agencies to provide price support to the 
farmers.  Cotton and Jute are also procured by Government at MSP through Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI) and Jute Corporation of India (JCI). Sugarcane is procured 
at Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), recommended by the Commission for 
Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) and approved by the Government before the 
start of each sugarcane season. 
  

 
 
The procurement of agricultural produce has expanded beyond wheat and rice 
to pulses, oilseeds and horticulture produce through PM-AASHA Scheme. 
Procurement of oilseeds (groundnut, soybean, sunflower, sesamum, niger seed, 
rapeseed/ mustard, safflower), pulses (arhar, moong, urad, gram & masur) and copra 
is done under Price Support Scheme under umbrella scheme of Pradhan Mantri 
Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA), on the request of the concerned 
State Government as per the guidelines as and when market price of these produce 
fall below the MSP. Further, Price Deficit Payment Scheme (PDPS) component 
envisages direct payment of the difference between the MSP and the selling / modal 
price to pre-registered farmers selling oilseeds of prescribed FAQ norms within the 
stipulated period in the notified market yard through a transparent auction process.  
Government also implements Market Intervention Scheme (MIS), a 
component under PM-AASHA, for procurement of agricultural and horticultural 
commodities, which are perishable in nature and are not covered under the MSP 
regime. The objective of intervention is to protect the growers of these commodities 
from making distress sale in the event of a bumper crop during the peak arrival period 
when the prices tend to fall below economic levels and the cost of production. There 
should be at least a 10 percent decrease in the ruling market prices over the previous 
normal year. The scheme is implemented at the request of a State/UT government.  
Government has introduced a new component of Price Differential Payment 
(PDP) under Market intervention scheme (MIS) from 2024-25 season for direct 
payment of the price difference between the Market Intervention Price (MIP) and the 
selling price to the farmers of perishable crops. States/UTs have an option to choose 
either to do physical procurement of the crop or to make the differential payment 
between the MIP & Sale Price to the farmers.  
Further, from 2024-25 season, Government added another component under 
Market intervention scheme (MIS) for reimbursing the Storage and Transportation cost 
of TOP crops (Tomato, Onion and Potato) to central nodal agencies & State 
designated agencies for transporting them from the producing State to consuming 
states in the interest of the farmers.  
    The Department of Consumer Affairs administers the Price Stabilisation Fund 
component of integrated PM-AASHA under which procurement is undertaken to 
maintain the buffer stocks of major pulses such as Tur, Urad, Chana, Moong, Masur 
and Onion.  
  

(d):   Agriculture is a State subject. Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
States through a comprehensive range of Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes and Programmes aimed at increasing production, productivity, farmers’ 
income etc across the country. These schemes encompass entire spectrum of 
agriculture, including credit, insurance, income support, infrastructure, crops (including 
horticulture), seeds, mechanization, marketing, organic and natural farming, farmer 
collectives, irrigation, extension, digital agriculture and procurement of crops. The list 
of schemes is placed at Annexure-III. The schemes are implemented on a continuous 
basis subject to budgetary provisions approved by the Parliament from time to time. 
      Further, the Government has substantially increased the budget allocation of 
Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare from ₹27,662.67 crore BE during 2013-14 
to ₹1,40,416.57 crore BE during 2026-27.
